title: How Filters Create Fake Links
objective: After this level you can explain how studying only a selected group can create a link between two traits that isn't there in everyone.
summary: SAT verbal and math scores rise together, but behind a 1320 admission cutoff the link flips. Filtering on two traits can create a false link, as Berkson saw with hospital patients.

cards.headline: At a picky college, the math stars seem to be weaker readers. Why?
cards.body: Is math crowding out words? No. The pattern among the students is real, but nothing in their heads makes it. It comes from the gate they all had to pass through.

cards.headline: A link made by a gate
cards.body: Allen Downey used real SAT data. Across test-takers, verbal and math scores rise together: strong at one usually means strong at the other. Then he imagined a college that admits only combined scores of 1320 or more. Among its students, the link flips: higher verbal scores go with lower math scores. Same kind of people, just filtered.

cards.headline: Why the gate flips it
cards.body: To get in with a so-so math score, you needed a great verbal score, and the reverse. Students weak at both never made it, so they're missing from the picture. Statisticians who study admissions describe the same pattern: an admitted student with an unusually low test score is more likely to have exceptional reference letters.

cards.fact: Filter a group on two traits, and a false link between them can appear.
cards.context: Joseph Berkson spotted this in 1946 with hospital patients. Being admitted depends on having some illness, so studying only patients can make a disease seem linked to a cause when it isn't. Before trusting a link, ask who was let through the gate, and who was left outside it.

mascot.line: This is Chapter 1's question again: out of what? A link found only among the filtered may not hold for everyone.

cards.headline: Filters: exposed
learned: Across test-takers, verbal and math rise together
Behind a 1320 cutoff, the link flips
Ask who got through the gate

questions.prompt: Match each with where they saw a filter create a link.
questions.explanation: Allen Downey used real SAT data, Joseph Berkson studied hospital patients in 1946, and statisticians who study admissions found low test scores going with exceptional reference letters.

questions.prompt: A talent show lets through only acts that are very funny, very skilled, or both. Among the finalists, the funniest acts seem the least skilled. Why?

options.label: Funny people practice less
options.rationale: No need for that story; the filter explains it.

options.label: It proves that humor and skill can never go together
options.rationale: Acts weak at both were filtered out, which creates the pattern.

options.label: The filter let in acts strong at one or the other
Judges secretly prefer skill
options.rationale: The pattern appears even with fair judges.

questions.explanation: An act with less skill needed lots of humor to get through, and the reverse, so the gate itself creates the link.

questions.prompt: The first question for any share is "out of what?" In Downey's flipped SAT link, what is the "out of what"?

options.label: Every student in the country who took the SAT
options.rationale: Across all test-takers, the scores rise together.

options.label: Exactly 100 students
options.rationale: The group is defined by the cutoff, not a round number.

options.label: All colleges in the country
options.rationale: The flip appears inside one filtered college.

options.label: Only students who passed the admission cutoff

questions.explanation: The flipped link holds only among students with combined scores of 1320 or more. Out of everyone, the link runs the other way.
